passage: Tuition teacher's note. Ayesha has been putting aside her pocket money for six weeks to buy a toy castle. Today at the shop window she stopped and stood for a long time. "Will I still play with it in a month?" she said quietly. She looked at the picture of the castle stuck on her notebook cover. After some thought she told me, "I think a book series and an art set will last longer." She crossed out the castle and wrote two new lines. I did not push her either way. She seemed calm about it, and took her time. Kalyani, tuition teacher.

qa.q: How long had Ayesha been saving?
qa.a: Ayesha had been saving for six weeks.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel as she stood at the shop window and changed her plan?
qa.a: Ayesha felt unsure whether she would still want the castle in a month, then calm about switching; the note says she seemed calm and took her time.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ayesha use to test the want, and why?
qa.a: Ayesha could wait another week and see if she still wants it, or ask a friend how long they played with theirs. Time shows whether a want lasts.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Ayesha's choice?
qa.a: Kalyani watched and chose not to push, so Kalyani sees a child making a calm, thoughtful choice without a grown-up steering it.

grounding: After saving for six weeks, a girl asks herself if she will still play with the toy in a month and decides a book series and art set are a better use of the money.

passage:
Saturday
Six weeks of saving for the robot dog that barks and does a flip. Today I held my tin and thought: after the first week, will I still play with it? Hemant bhaiya's robot car has been under his bed, dusty, since Holi. I tried to picture next month: me, and the robot dog sitting on the shelf. Then I looked at my other shelf. The mystery books I love, and my old broken crayons. I'd read a new book series again and again. I'd draw every day. So I've changed my mind. The money is going to the five-book mystery set and a proper art box. Maa said, 'Gargi beti, that's a grown-up choice.' I feel light.

qa.q: Where has Hemant's robot car been since Holi?
How does Gargi feel after changing her mind?
qa.a: Gargi feels relieved and sure, having chosen things she'll use every day.

qa.q: What question helped Gargi decide, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Whether she'd still play with the toy after a month; picturing next month showed which choice would last.

qa.q: How might Maa see Gargi's choice?
qa.a: Maa calls it a grown-up choice, so she seems proud of how Gargi thought it through.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after six weeks of saving, asks whether she'll still play with the toy in a month and chooses books and an art set instead.

passage: For six weeks Gargi had saved her coins in a clay pot, all for the wind-up toy train at the stall near the bus stand. On the evening of the Dussehra mela she walked there with her brother Vaibhav, the money knotted in her dupatta. The train went round its little track, bright red. Gargi watched it, then remembered Vaibhav's spinning top from last year, lost in the cowshed within a month. Would she still play with the train after the mela? She looked at the next stall: a set of four Hindi storybooks and a box of wax crayons. She'd read those till the pages went soft. "Books and crayons," she said. Vaibhav stared. "Not the train?" Gargi shook her head, already choosing the first book.

qa.q: Where had Gargi saved her coins?
What was Gargi thinking as she watched the train?
qa.a: She felt unsure, remembering Vaibhav's lost spinning top, and wondered whether she'd still play with the train after the mela.

qa.q: Why was thinking again before spending a wise step?
qa.a: It helped her pick books and crayons she'd use for a long time, instead of a toy she might forget within a month.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Gargi's choice?
qa.a: Vaibhav stares and asks 'Not the train?', so he's surprised she changed her mind.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who has saved for weeks rethinking whether she'll still want the toy in a month, and choosing storybooks and crayons.
